title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with a synthetic likeness. Someone on a WhatsApp video call presented a face and voice made to resemble a sitting chief minister, and the fraud depended on the target believing that the person he could see and hear was that public figure. The AI did not make a false claim in text, it manufactured a person. The script around it, a manager, an allotted sum, a CBI officer and a fine, was ordinary social engineering that the fabricated identity made credible.

The failure sits at the point where a consumer messaging app carries a live call without authenticating who is on the other end. Nothing in the call itself distinguished a generated face from a real one, and the payments moved through a digital payment app that had no reason to question them. Catching it would have required confirming the caller's identity through a channel independent of the call, or establishing that the aid programme and the fees attached to it existed. The sums were small and sequential, which is what let the total reach over Rs 1.04 lakh before the victim refused a further demand.

What is not established is who placed the call, whether those people generated the likeness themselves, or whether anyone will be convicted. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act, and a registration is not a finding. The account rests on a single outlet's reporting.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29-year-old security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on September 9 from someone using an AI deepfake to look and sound like Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay. The caller offered him Rs 11 lakh in financial aid. A supposed manager said Rs 5 lakh was allotted and asked for small fees. Giri first paid Rs 5,000 as exchange charges, then Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN. A person claiming to be a CBI officer named Thakur demanded more than Rs 50,000 as a fine. Giri paid over Rs 1.04 lakh in total through a digital payment app.

When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, Giri refused and realized he had been cheated. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then approached Byappanahalli police. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act. Police said this was the first such case reported in the city and urged people not to believe such calls or make payments based on them.
